stops.name: Tokyo Tower
stops.en: This was a newly re-industrialized Japan's 1958 answer to Paris's Eiffel Tower — a bit more modern-looking and 9 m taller. Entry to the Main Observatory (150m) is ¥820, while ascending to the Special Observatory (250m) is an extra ¥600. Your photo will be taken for purchase later (¥600). Tip: To get a good view of, and picture with, the tower, try the courtyard in front of Zojoji

stops.name: Yasukuni Shrine
stops.en: A controversial shrine to Japan's war dead, housing the souls of some 2.5 million people killed in Japan's wars — including convicted war criminals executed by the Allies. A favorite haunt of right-wing groups in black loudspeaker-equipped trucks, and often visited by Japanese and Taiwanese politicians, drawing sharp criticisms from neighbors China and South Korea in the process. Consider ke

stops.name: Tokyo Imperial Palace
stops.en: Surrounded by a series of moats and high walls, the site of the former Edo Castle has been the official residence of the Japanese imperial family since 1868. Reputedly the most expensive square kilometre in the world, which during the height of Japan's bubble was estimated to be worth slightly more than California. The inner palace gardens and buildings are closed to the general public except on t

stops.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
stops.en: The two enormous buildings of this giant hive of bureaucracy are an Orwellian architectural masterpiece designed by noted architect Kenzo Tange. The main reasons to come here, though, are the twin observatories. At a height of 202 m on the 45th floor, they have some of the best views of Tokyo. The North Observatory is open daily from 09:30 to 23:00 (closed second and fourth Mondays of each month),

stops.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
stops.en: Seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Tokyo. Designed by the famous architect Tange Kenzō, this ultramodern church was built in the 1960s to replace an older structure that was destroyed during the war.

stops.name: National Diet Building
stops.en: Housing Japan's bicameral legislature, it was built in the 1920s. The most recognizable symbol of the Japanese government, it was built from Japanese building materials, features a pyramidal roof and is surrounded with green areas. The nearby free Kensei Kinenkan (between the Diet and the water) has a nice view on it, and tons of political artefacts to satisfy those interested in Japanese politics

stops.name: Shinjuku Gyoen
stops.en: A large public garden, and one of the most popular places for viewing cherry blossoms in spring. It has Japanese, English and French gardens, as well as a Taiwanese teahouse and a greenhouse. The entrance fee often makes the park surprisingly uncrowded and peaceful. Admission ends 30 minutes before closing.

stops.name: The National Museum of Modern Art
stops.en: With a modest permanent collection on display and regularly changing exhibitions, MOMAT is a nice place to kill a couple of hours after you've seen the Imperial Palace across the road. Entry to the nearby Crafts Gallery is included in the price.

stops.name: Hamarikyu Gardens
stops.en: It was built by 17th-century shoguns for their private enjoyment. Hama-rikyu is now a public walking garden with an all-season range of flowers and flowering trees. The highlight is the tea house, picturesquely set on a small island in the middle of a pond, where green tea and sweets are available starting at ¥500, and ¥1000 for a set. The garden is next to Tsukiji fish market. A boat which runs u

stops.name: Holy Resurrection Cathedral
stops.en: A beautifully-restored 1800s-vintage Russian Orthodox cathedral located near Ochanomizu Station on the Chuo Line. Use the Hijiribashi exit. The Hijiribashi bridge by the exit is one of the better looking bridges in Tokyo and looks moderately attractive when lit-up at night.

stops.name: Kanda-myōjin
stops.en: This shrine has a history dating back to the 8th century and had been highly regarded under the Edo shogunate. The current red-pillared structure has been rebuilt after being completely destroyed in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. The Kanda Matsuri festival, which takes place in mid-May every other year is one of the largest in Tokyo and is a sight to behold. Arrive before noon or the shrine gets

stops.name: Zōjō-ji Temple
stops.en: This grand old temple is the headquarters of the Jōdo-shū sect and houses the graves of 6 of the Tokugawa shoguns, but is a little off the beaten track and is rarely visited by tourists. Particularly beautiful around cherry blossom time. It hosts a variety of religious and non-religious festivals throughout the year.

stops.name: Rikugi Garden
stops.en: A classical Japanese park with ponds, hills and teahouses, that was built in 1695 by Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu, a Tokugawa daimyo. It's a popular cherry blossom spot in spring and is lit up at night at this time.

stops.name: Koishikawa Botanical Garden
stops.local: 東京大学大学院理学系研究科附属植物園
stops.en: Not one of the great gardens of Japan and sometimes a bit shabby, but a pleasant stroll with interesting trees, a medicinal herb garden and several ponds. Not to be confused with Koishikawa Korakuen.

stops.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Teien Art Museum
stops.en: Art museum housed in a classic Art Deco style structure, connected to a small park with Japanese and Western gardens and outdoor sculptures.

stops.name: Tsukiji Hongan-ji Temple
stops.en: A Jōdo Shinshū temple just a few blocks away from the fish market, worth seeing because of its unique, South Asian-inspired architecture. Buddhist services are held in English on Saturday evenings.

stops.name: Koishikawa Kōrakuen Garden
stops.en: Laid out in the 17th century, this splendid traditional garden boasts a large collection of trees and flowering plants that provide touches of beauty all year round. Winding paths, wooded hills, ponds teeming with ducks and fish. The place can be a little crowded at certain times of year (such as during the cherry blossom season in late March-mid April), but there's plenty of room for everyone.

stops.name: Yushima Seidō
stops.en: A temple of Confucius.

stops.name: Japanese Folk Crafts Museum
stops.en: Founded in 1936. Must see for Japanese handicraft lovers.

stops.name: Institute for Nature Study
stops.local: 国立科学博物館附属自然教育園
stops.en: A 200,000 sq m nature preserve in the heart of the city, with birds and waterfowl, insects and marine life.

stops.name: Kōgan-ji Temple
stops.en: This small temple in Sugamo is known for two statues: Togenuki Jizō, who heals sick children, and the boddhisattva Kannon, who will cure your pains if you wash themagical appropriate part of the statue. More morbidly, you can also pray to Kannon for a swift and painless death, so you will not be a burden to your relatives in your old age. Visitors pray Enmei Jizōson for their health too. The way t

stops.name: Asakura Museum of Sculpture
stops.en: 20px|Must visit! Sculptor Asakura Fumio (Artist name Kōso 1883-1964) designed this atmospheric house himself. It combined his original Japanese home and garden with a large studio that incorporated vaulted ceilings, a 'sunrise room' and a rooftop garden with wonderful neighbourhood views. It's now a reverential museum with many artist's signature realist works, mostly of people and cats, on displa

stops.name: Hijiri-bashi bridge
stops.en: On the Kanda river (神田川), on the border between Bunkyō and Chiyoda wards. It offers one of the best spots in Tokyo to see trains, three lines crossing each other (on the west, so better seen in the afternoon). Akihabara district in 500 m/10 min away to the east. Its name means Saints bridge. One side at Temple of Confucius Yushima Seido (湯島聖堂), the other side at cathedral of the Japanese Orthodox

stops.name: Mode Gakuen Cocoon Tower
stops.local: モード学園コクーンタワー

stops.name: Tokyo Skytree
stops.en: Completed in 2012, Tokyo Skytree stands tall over the old Sumida ward as the newest symbol of Tokyo and the world's tallest self-supporting tower at 634 m. It is the primary location from which digital television broadcast signals in Tokyo are transmitted. The tower's LED lighting system uses a different color scheme every night. The Skytree is complemented by a shopping complex, Tokyo Solamachi (

stops.name: Hachikō
stops.en: A diminutive statue of a dog tucked away in one corner of the big plaza outside the station, best known as a meeting place and for the story (see box). It is also the name of one of the many exits from Shibuya Station and the prime meeting place before a night out. Just hanging out near Hachiko for a while will give you some great people-watching.

stops.name: Tokyo Stock Exchange
stops.en: Tokyo's stock exchange, while one of the largest in the world by capitalization, is now entirely automated, and the tiny building it resides in is mostly for show, featuring a small museum, exhibition hall, and broadcasting facilities. English tours can be booked in advance.

stops.name: House of Councillors to the Emperor
Tsukiji fish market
stops.en: For more than 80 years, Tsukiji was the world's largest wholesale fish market. Although the wholesale operations (including the famous tuna auctions) closed in 2018 and moved to Toyosu, the outer market remains in place and continues to welcome the public with stalls selling fresh fish, sushi, produce and kitchen supplies. Suggested plans for the former inner market site include a sport stadium or

stops.name: Rainbow Bridge
stops.en: Completed in 1993, this gateway to Odaiba is among the most beautiful modern bridges in Japan. Decorated with 444 lights, which change according to the seasons. Can be crossed by bus or metro.

stops.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan
Tokyo International Forum
stops.en: A massive, modern exhibition centre used for concerts, conventions and the like. On weekdays there are usually several food wagons selling boxed lunches, but aside from this there may not be much of interest to the casual tourist — except, of course, the impressive design. The atrium may be the most well-known symbol of the building, and one is able to stroll up the long, spiral walkway that runs

stops.name: Shibuya scramble crossing
stops.local: 渋谷スクランブル交差点
stops.en: The famous crossing sees people crossing in every direction en masse. The second floor of the Starbucks has been a great spot to take photos of the crazy pedestrian crossing. The coffee shop closed in 2023 for renovation of the building and is due to reopen late April 2024 with a larger cafe/lounge.

stops.name: NTT Docomo Yoyogi Building
stops.en: This gigantic tower resembling a granite Empire State Building, south of the Shinjuku Station, is owned by NTT DoCoMo, Japan's largest cell-phone carrier. The upper part of the building is a mobile communications tower.

stops.name: Sunshine 60
stops.en: Sunshine 60 was once the tallest building in Japan and it remains the most prominent building within the Sunshine City complex. The surrounding Sunshine City complex includes shops, restaurants, an aquarium, and an observatory at the top of the Sunshine 60 building.

stops.name: Tokyo Opera City Tower
stops.en: A building complex with a skyscraper. Housing the New National Theatre Tokyo, concert halls, two art museums (one specialized in multimedia art), many shops and restaurants.

stops.name: Edo-Tokyo Museum
stops.local: 東京都江戸東京博物館
stops.en: This bizarre multi-story edifice suspended in midair and bearing not a small resemblance to a Star Wars Imperial Walker (meant to be a replica of an old raised warehouse) covers the history of the metropolis, starting from 1590 when it was selected as Japan's new capital Edo, all the way through the Kanto earthquake and firebombings of World War II. The museum is built with the latest technology i

stops.name: National Theatre of Japan
stops.en: For those interested in theatre arts, the Kokuritsu Gekijyo holds performances in traditional arts ranging from Kabuki, Noh drama, Bunraku puppet theatre, etc. You may want to check the schedule and make a reservation beforehand.

stops.name: Kitanomaru Park
stops.en: Connected to the East Gardens on the north side is this park. Offering much of the same, it is a convenient way to get to Yasukuni Shrine. The park also houses the Nippon Budōkan (日本武道館), which regularly stages martial arts competitions and live concerts, as well as the Kagaku Gijyutsukan (科学技術館, Science museum).

stops.name: Hie Shrine
stops.en: Another prominent shrine in Tokyo. Located atop a little hill at the edge of the area. Reached by a steep flight of stairs under a veritable tunnel of orange torii, the shrine grounds are an oasis of tranquility in the middle of Tokyo and, in good weather, a popular place for a lunchtime picnic. The Sanno Matsuri (山王祭) festival it hosts in June is counted among the 3 Great festival of Tokyo, featu

stops.name: Sengaku-ji Temple
stops.en: A temple most famous as the resting place of the 47 Rōnin, a famous group of samurai who banded together to avenge their unfairly slain master. Having obtained the head of the offender, they brought it to this very temple and then were condemned to commit ritual suicide, like their master. The story is told in Chūshingura, the best-known of all Kabuki plays. History aside, the temple isn't much to

stops.name: Nezu Museum
stops.en: Showcases the private art collection of Nezu Kaichirō with many pieces from the Edo period.

stops.name: Tōyō Bunko
stops.en: The Toyo Bunko is a special library and a research institute of Oriental studies. The research focuses on Asian history and cultures. The Toyo Bunko collects and saves historical records of Asia. The collection of books exceeds 950,000 items. People can read the books free of charge. Library materials cannot leave the building. Photocopiers are available for use at a minimal charge.

stops.name: Tokyo Midtown
stops.en: Opened in April 2007, this competitor to Roppongi Hills boasts Tokyo's second tallest office building, a Ritz-Carlton and yet more endless acres of shopping and eating. Still, Midtown favors wood paneling and greenery over raw concrete and feels a little more human than Hills do. The main gallery (and the floor under) always have open Japanese art exhibits.

stops.name: Yūshūkan
stops.en: An odd collection of military paraphernalia (including human torpedoes and letters from kamikaze pilots) and one-sided (allegedly revisionist according to the Chinese, Koreans and other Asian countries except Taiwan) descriptions of Imperial Japan and World War II, but it can be pretty confronting at times. The museum includes a small military history book and model shop.

stops.name: Mitsui Memorial Museum
stops.en: Art museum, the collection includes items used in the Japanese tea ceremony as well as Eastern antiques. Housed in an historic building dating back to 1926.

stops.name: Suntory Museum of Art
stops.en: Hosts changing art exhibitions.

stops.name: Idemitsu Museum of Arts
stops.en: Has a noteworthy collection centering on Japanese traditional arts.

stops.name: Yamatane Museum of Art
stops.en: Specializes in modern Japanese-style paintings and has a notable collection, though only a handful are on display at one time due to preservation issues.

stops.name: Sony Building
stops.en: The Sony Showroom has four floors of the latest Sony products, with a small shop on the 3rd floor. The building also houses a BMW showroom.

stops.name: 21 21 DESIGN SIGHT
stops.en: Changing exhibitions devoted to the latest and greatest in Japanese design.

stops.name: Hanazono Shrine
stops.en: More remarkable for its location than its appearance, but it's a nice place to take a breather. There's often a flea market in the surrounding park on weekends.

stops.name: Hara Museum of Contemporary Art
stops.en: This small museum hosts a variety of interesting exhibitions in a 1930s house which is a great example of modern architecture in pre-war Japan. There is a very nice indoor/outdoor cafe. (2026: closed/moved to Gunma prefecture, see Wikipedia)

stops.name: Japanese Sword Museum
stops.en: Display of all types of Japanese art swords and fittings, some of them centuries old. Beautiful view from balcony on 3rd floor over Kyū Yasuda Garden. Quite hefty entrance fee, but a must see for anyone interested in Japanese swords.

stops.name: Bunkyo Civic Center
stops.en: The lavish government building for the Bunkyo ward of Tokyo, once described in the Japan Times as "a colossal Pez candy dispenser." A free observation deck on the 25th floor, jutting out of the top like the Starship Enterprise, commands a fine view of much of Tokyo.

stops.name: Zōshigaya Cemetery
stops.en: The final resting place of Lafcadio Hearn is about the most exciting attraction in this neck of the woods.

stops.name: Jōkan-ji Temple
stops.en: Arguably the most visible reminder of the tragedy of the lives of the prostitutes who lived and worked in Yoshiwara. This is where many of the prostitutes were buried when they died, as the brothels would just unceremoniously dump their corpses at the back entrance to the temple.

stops.name: Chidori-ga-fuchi moat
stops.en: One of, if not the most prominent cherry blossom site in Tokyo, and attracts throngs of people in its March-to-April peak season. It is located just across the street from Yasukuni-shrine. Rowboats are also available for one to row along a limited portion of the moat at ¥500 for 30 minutes, ¥1000 for an hour and at a slightly more expensive rate during cherry blossom periods.

stops.name: Aqua Park Shinagawa
stops.en: A popular aquarium with exhibits that combine dolphin shows and technology. The tunnel tank includes manta rays, green sawfish, and the only dwarf sawfish on display in the world.

stops.name: Tokyo Anime Center
stops.en: Offers information, showings, demonstrations, and events centered around animation and gaming. In the recording studio, visitors can experience a post-recording on certain days.

stops.name: Tobacco and Salt Museum
stops.en: This peculiar institution owes its existence to Japan's government monopoly on these two substances. The website advises that "dangerous substances are not permitted within the museum". They have map-guides of the museum in English and most exhibits have English translations. There is a free mobile-app based auto tour as well.

stops.name: Sumo Museum
stops.en: A small, quirky museum tucked inside the arena's first floor, dedicated to the history of sumo, particularly artifacts and ceremonial clothing, almost entirely in Japanese only. The collection rotates several times a year. During sumo tournaments, it is open daily, but only to tournament ticket holders.

stops.name: Fire Museum
stops.en: Three fire-fighting helicopters, ten trucks, and 3 floors of exhibitions. Very popular with kids, who can wear fire-fighting clothes and ride some of the helicopters and trucks.

stops.name: Taro Okamoto Memorial Museum
stops.en: Former studio and house of Okamoto Taro. Unfinished works and paintings are shown. He made numerous masterpieces such as "Tower of the Sun" at the Expo 1970 and "Myth of the Future" mural now exhibited in Shibuya.

stops.name: Nogi shrine
stops.en: General Nogi's house is a great example of Western architecture constructed during the Meiji period (19th century), mixing Japanese and Western elements. The general killed himself here after the Meiji Emperor's death. Descend the stairs to reach the shrine that was dedicated to him in 1917. Lonely place, very photogenic.

stops.name: TEPIA
stops.en: Science museum showcasing new technologies, robots, home automation. Explanations are in Japanese but playing with the objects is still fun for kids and adults.

stops.name: Hōmyō-ji Temple
stops.en: Famous Japanese temple built in 810. Features the statue of Kishimojin (鬼子母神像) who is a Japanese God of fertility. Visitors go to Hōmyōji to pray for their children's birth, growth and security. The Kishimojin figure typically take the form of the devil, but this statue holds a baby, and the figure is beautiful. In this temple the Oeshiki-Taisai festival (御会式大祭) is held from October 16 to October

stops.name: Kumano Shrine
stops.en: Built 800 years ago. Surrounded by trees, people visit to pray or just for the peace and quiet. Some come for specific the worship practice of Yakuyoke, a purification ritual to drive out evil spirits. Like all shrines, they sell protective amulets for health, good studies, or traffic safety, but these are distinctively cute. For a traditional shrine, they have a particularly flashy website that g

stops.name: Myōgyō-ji Temple
stops.en: According to legend, the grave of Lady Oiwa (Oiwa-san) in Yotsuya Kaidan, Japan's best-known ghost story and a direct inspiration for the Ring horror movies, is in this temple. In a nutshell, the beautiful Oiwa was disfigured, divorced and killed, and then comes back to haunt the people who wronged her.

stops.name: Mori Building Digital Art Museum: EPSON teamLab Borderless
stops.en: Art museum with immersive art exhibits.

stops.name: Shitamachi Museum Annex
stops.en: Many buildings scattered around the Yanaka district survived the bombings of World War II, including this former sake store built in 1910. Characteristic of Meiji-era architecture, the building now houses a small museum of sake and beer equipment.

stops.name: Shinjuku-sanchōme and related red-light districts to the east of the station
stops.en: It is perfectly safe to walk around here during the day and marvel at the photo billboards of various male and female escorts on offer as well as the live gangster-types acting shady. While it probably shouldn't be done with children, for adults the result is far more "cultural interest" than sleaze.

stops.name: Shinjuku Southern Terrace
stops.en: The promenade next to the Southern Terrace exit offers a magnificent view of the Takashimaya department store and a bridge that offers the best spot for watching trains enter and exit. Starbucks, Shake Shack and other restaurants.

stops.name: Tokyo Toy Museum
stops.en: An old school filled with toys and fun small houses. Accompanying adults won't get bored, thanks to the variety of toys.

stops.name: Suga Shrine
stops.en: It is a shrine located around Shinjuku. It is a small shrine, but the stairs in front of it are famous as the background in the animated movie Your Name.

stops.name: mAAch ecute Kanda Manseibashi
stops.en: A historic train station that's been converted into a shopping mall. Besides interesting shops and cafes, there's also a library and history exhibits about the station, including a large diorama showing the area around the station as it was in 1912 when it opened.

stops.name: Imperial Palace East Garden
stops.en: Kept in impeccable shape, the gardens of the Imperial Palace are particularly beautiful during the March and April plum and cherry blossom seasons. During the Edo period, this was the heart of the Shogun's castle, and you can see the tenshudai, the raised platform where the tenshukaku (main keep) was once located, and an open field that was once the site of the honmaru goten, the Shogun's main res

stops.name: Nihonbashi Bridge
stops.en: Nihonbashi means Japan bridge. It is the most famous bridge in Japan and one of the very few historic bridges remaining in Tokyo. The current stone and steel bridge was built in 1911. It is the point from which all distances are measured to the capital. Since 1964 it is unfortunately overshadowed by a massive expressway, blocking much of the view.

stops.name: Japan Traditional Crafts Aoyama Square
stops.en: Gallery and shop for handicraft products from all over Japan.

stops.name: Center Gai
stops.en: The narrow street leading away from the station to the left of the giant video screen, it's famous as the birthplace of many of Japan's youth fashion trends. Center Gai is jam-packed with clothing stores, music stores, and video game arcades. This is a great place to stroll and feel the Shibuya vibe.

stops.name: Moyai statues
stops.en: Another popular meeting spot, this time on the south side of the station, the two Moyai statues here are a spin on Easter Island's famous moai, made from volcanic pumice on Niijima in the Izu Islands far south of Tokyo. This, not the originals, was the inspiration for the 🗿 emoji.

stops.name: Bunkamura
stops.en: Bunkamura-dori. A complex featuring an excellent art museum, in addition to theaters for film and stage plays. On the basement floor there's an art and design bookstore as well as a branch of Paris' famous Les Deux Magots café.

stops.name: Hikarie
stops.en: Hikarie is a massive building on the east side of Shibuya Station with many restaurants, galleries, and theaters. Opened in 2012.

stops.name: Myth of Tomorrow
stops.en: A huge mural by famous artist Tarō Okamoto, it commemorates the Hiroshima atomic bombing. A human figure in it burns and others appear to run from flames. The mural is at the entrance of the Inokashira line, 100 m from Hachikō. It was built in Mexico, found there in 2004 and brought to Japan in 2005. Under repair from Oct 2023.

stops.name: Showa Neon Takamura Kanban Museum
stops.en: The sign company Showa Neon has a museum with shop signs from the Edo and early Meiji periods. Reportedly all descriptions in this museum are in Japanese. Closed in June 2023 for renovation; reopen due in March 2025.

stops.name: Honmyōji Temple
stops.en: This temple is known for a fire called Meireki-no-Taika, an inferno 400 years ago which killed over 100,000 people. It is said that this fire broke out in Honmyōji. There are also some tombs of famous people in this temple. A Japanese swordman Chiba Shūsaku and a political office leader Tōyama Kinshirō, for example.

stops.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre
stops.en: Offers various exhibits and concerts behind the impressive glass facade.

stops.name: Tokyo Shaheed Minar
stops.en: A beautiful monument, symbolizing love to the mother language. It is based on the mother language movement, that originated in Dhaka, Bangladesh in 1952, followed by the UNESCO declaration of International Mother Language Day (21 February). It was a present from Bangladesh to the Japanese people, in 2005, recognizing Tokyo Boishakhi Mela (Bangladesh New Year Festival), organized every year in mid

stops.name: Meguro Parasitological Museum
stops.en: One of a kind and oddly popular with couples on dates, although you might want to skip lunch before (or after) your visit here as the exhibits and pictures can be rather graphic. A compact two-story building, the most famous exhibit inside is an 8.8-meter-long tapeworm, with a matching string for you to take the measurement.

stops.name: Meguro Gajoen
stops.en: A luxury hotel and wedding hall, with restaurants, cafes, and banquet rooms. One of the most popular attractions, though, is the spectacular public restroom.

stops.name: Gohyakurakanji
stops.en: This temple contains over 300 statues, all with different facial expressions. They were all carved by the same monk from 1687 to 1695.

stops.name: SCAI The Bathhouse
stops.en: A small gallery showing the work of contemporary artists, the building is a former sento, or bathhouse.

stops.name: AKB48 theater
stops.en: AKB48 is a home-grown, all-girl idol group — their name comes from Akihabara — which started in 2005 and quickly became the best-selling female group in Japan. They perform 6 days a week. If you are into J-pop music and cute girls all rolled into one (and are lucky enough to win the ticket lottery), don't miss this.

stops.name: Kanda Myojin Shrine
stops.en: Akihabara's own temple. You can buy a multi-piece charm for ¥1,000 which will protect your electronic devices from evil. It's mostly noteworthy for the festival it organizes around May. On this occasion, a massive shrine is traditionally carried through the streets of Akihabara, providing an interesting contrast with all the high-tech to say the least.

stops.name: Taito Station
stops.en: Another arcade, "Hey" on Chuo Dori is also run by Taito.

stops.name: GiGO
stops.en: Formerly run by Sega, four locations in Akihabara. As of July 31, 2025, the first store of gigo was closed.

stops.name: San-ai Building
stops.en: Closed in 2023 for rebuilding, reopen due 2027. The heart of Ginza is the intersection of Chuo-dori and Harumi-dori, dominated by the glass cylinder of this building. With its huge neon sign, it's been the image of Ginza on postcards and travel books for decades now. The other corners are occupied by Wako and Mitsukoshi, two of the most prestigious department stores (the former being a cut above),

stops.name: Ginza Blossom
stops.en: This theater hosts a variety of different events. See the website for a partial listing.

stops.name: Fujifilm Square
stops.en: Fujifilm's exhibition space for the latest and greatest in photography. Exhibits are usually free and well worth a visit.

eats.name: Pasutakan
eats.note: Okonomiyaki cooked at your table.

eats.name: Khao San
eats.note: A good place for Thai street-stall style food. It's always packed and hectic for lunch, with attendants hollering to attract customers.

eats.name: Blumare
eats.note: Pizza and pasta restaurant. The building is full of restaurants all run by Sapporo Beer.

eats.name: Suzuya
eats.note: This tonkatsu restaurant is famous for its green tea tonkatsu, which is salty and filling. It also serves other types of tonkatsu and katsudon.

eats.name: Martiniburger
eats.note: This restaurant serves hamburgers and martinis. The large juicy hamburgers are made with high quality ground beef, which is very hard to find anywhere in Japan. Though uncommon, the combination of ham

eats.name: Acacia Shinjuku
eats.note: Specializes in cabbage rolls. Also has a set menu with hashed rice and pork sauté. Has a branch at Haneda Airport.

eats.name: Botejyu
eats.note: Botejyu is an okonomiyaki shop that sells a variety of okonomiyaki. They also have various yaki-soba dishes. Beware that at times, this restaurant can be busy with wait times of up to 30 min.

eats.name: Juttoku
eats.note: This izakaya has an excellent selection of sake.

eats.name: Kappō Nakajima
eats.note: Specializes in sardine dishes. Yanagawa teishoku is deep-fried sardines with scrambled eggs on rice (it tastes better than it sounds).

eats.name: Hokkaido
eats.note: Enjoy the view while dining on seafood and other specialties of Hokkaido. Got another branch near Shinjuku station (9F 110 Building).

eats.name: Yanbaru
eats.note: Now occupying the whole of a three-story building, there's nothing pretentious about this restaurant specializing in Okinawan food, which emphasizes pork and vegetables that are unusual even to Honshu

eats.name: Bosphorus Hasan
eats.note: Authentic Turkish food. HALAL food.

eats.name: Din Tai Fung
eats.note: Tokyo branch of the renowned Taiwan dim sum restaurant; speciality is the xiǎolóngbāo () soup-in dumplings.

eats.name: Nabezo
eats.note: An all-you-can-eat Shabu Shabu restaurant with another branch in Shinjuku and many other places. \3850 gets one person 100 minutes, including unlimited meat, veggies, and ice cream. Drinks cost extra,

eats.name: Onegiya Shinjuku ten
eats.note: Excellent traditional but modern Japanese restaurant. Plenty of dishes to order but you need to like leeks.

eats.name: Zauo
eats.note: Indoor fishing and restaurant combined at dinner time...(click the link and see photos). No fishing on weekday lunch time.

eats.name: Kurukuru Wanko

eats.name: Torafugu-Tei

eats.name: Araku
eats.note: Australian-run, considerably larger and can be less intimidating than many other Golden Gai establishments.

eats.name: Bar K
eats.note: Always welcoming of foreigners with beers.

eats.name: Hair of The Dogs
eats.note: Punk rock with a dash of Mexican Luchadors. Good cocktails and beer at an average of ¥700 a drink. The owner, Tohru, is very welcoming to anyone who loves to rock. Cover charge lets you sit at the bar

eats.name: Bar Albatross-G
eats.note: Casual cocktail bar with Burgundy painted walls, chandeliers and no-frills mixology. Cover charge includes a small snack of either noodles, miso or whatever's brewing. Most drinks are around ¥700. Spa

eats.name: Rock Bar: Mother
eats.note: Has an extensive collection of Punk and Metal CDs for those looking for some alternative rock.

eats.name: Godz Bar
eats.note: Heavy metal/hard rock bar.

eats.name: Champion
eats.note: Staffed mostly by Filipinas who speak excellent English.

eats.name: New York Bar & Grill

eats.name: Casablanca
eats.note: A two level nightclub and lounge with a large dance floor and darts. The DJ normally spins hip-hop, R&B, reggae, and house, and there are live house performances periodically through the night.

eats.name: Loft/Plus One
eats.note: Performance art space meets bar run with a simple concept: different people and groups rent a block of time and do whatever they want to. The end result runs from stand-up comedy and lectures to porn

eats.name: Tokyo Loose
eats.note: Small bar full of men. It's not easy to find, so call for directions.

eats.name: Adezakura
eats.note: Lesbian bar.

eats.name: AiiRO Cafe
eats.note: Cruisy open-air bar with a torii gate at the entrance. Crowd spilling onto the street makes it feel like a block party.

eats.name: Arty Farty
eats.note: Among Nichō's most well-known pubs, with a thumping dance floor. A hand stamp upon entry will also get you into sister bar The Annex.

eats.name: Campy! Bar
eats.note: "Mix bar". Has another branch at Shibuya PARCO.

eats.name: Dragon Men
eats.note: Masculine gay pub with a dance floor. Rebuilt after a fire, the place is popular among male and female foreigners, and with Japanese men.

eats.name: GB
eats.note: Relaxed basement bar with somewhat more mature crowds.

eats.name: Gold Finger
eats.note: Primarily lesbian bar with all-female staff, and karaoke for the multinational patrons. Interior themed like a 1970s motel. Saturday is strictly women-only; Monday is FtM night.

eats.name: New Sazae
eats.note: Bar with dancefloor known for attracting bisexual crowds.

eats.name: Vox
eats.note: Another mix bar.

eats.name: Akha Ama
eats.note: Specialty coffee from northern Thailand.

eats.name: Doutor
eats.note: Doutor is a relatively "salary man" coffee shop. You will see lots of business men within this shop. Non-smoking, with some shops equipped with smoking booths.

eats.name: Excelsior Caffe

eats.name: Pronto/Di Punto
eats.note: Pronto is a very relaxed cafe/bar that is a cafe during the day. They offer premium style drinks.

eats.name: Segafredo Zanetti Espresso
eats.note: Segafredo is a somewhat upscale Italian style cafe that has various locations near Shinjuku. Segafredo tends to have a darker atmosphere akin to Pronto and offers many kinds of alcoholic drinks too.

eats.name: Canal Cafe

eats.name: Tajimaya Coffee house
eats.note: Truely classic kissaten (full-service coffee shop).

eats.name: Tokiya
eats.note: Japanese sweets and drinks. Famous for dorayaki, drum-shaped cake with red-bean paste inside.

eats.name: HUB

eats.name: Marone

eats.name: Vagabond
eats.note: A great little pub with two floors. The first floor is a little more private while the top floor is a very cozy jazz bar with live music and a good selection of finger foods cooked right at the bar fo

eats.name: Peter
eats.note: Restaurant with amazing views of Imperial Palace and excellent service. Lunch seems the best value. Kobe beef from ¥23,500. Dress code: casual.

eats.name: Yamaya
eats.note: For lunch you should get a bowl of rice with mentaiko (semi-spicy red fish eggs). Their specialty for dinner is motsunabe (tripe hotpot).

eats.name: Kanda Yabu soba
eats.note: Yabu Soba opened its doors for business in 1880.

eats.name: RyuGin

eats.name: Oshio Honten
eats.note: The original shop of one of the better-known chains here, with half a dozen restaurants. Try the mentaiko-shiso monja with cod roe and perilla, which tastes oh so much better than it looks.

eats.name: Sushisay Main Store
eats.note: Over 120 years old, this is now a large chain, but the head shop is in Tsukiji and it is well-reputed.

eats.name: Tamahide

eats.name: Tsujihan
eats.note: It is a Kaisen-dong store located near Tokyo Station. It is characterized by pouring stock with a little rice left.

eats.name: Daiei
eats.note: Two floors of food, drinks and more.

eats.name: Kua'aina
eats.note: Hawaiian hamburgers, order-at-the counter from a picture menu with English.

eats.name: Worldstar Cafe
eats.note: Popular with business people or singles during lunchtime. Meal sets are ¥980–1200, comes w/ main, salad, drink; main being spaghetti, etc. Useful for a late night spot to hang around, since they're op

eats.note: This lively and popular izakaya, with a spectacular spacious interior and high-profile location, has served luminaries such as George W. Bush and former Prime Minister Koizumi, and was the model for t

eats.name: Kushinobō
eats.note: for kushiage (deep-fried skewers).

eats.name: Nodaiwa

eats.note: This is a fashionable cafe of Paris style. You can enjoy elegant mood with seeing a row of houses and street of Omotesando. You can also choose fish or meat for lunch. Has another branch at Minato Mir

eats.name: Daigo

eats.name: Narisawa

eats.name: Ristorante da Nino
eats.note: Within easy walking distance from both Tokyo Midtown and Roppongi crossing, owner chef Antonino Lentini offers fine and fresh Sicilian dishes. Good wine selection.

eats.name: Kujiraya

eats.name: Murghi
eats.note: Founded in 1951, when the owner decided to serve the kind of curry he had enjoyed in Burma before World War II.

eats.name: Tokyu Food Show
eats.note: A superb food section in the basement with enough free samples to make a full lunch, if you don't mind not having a place to sit.

eats.name: Gonpachi
eats.note: Trendy foreigner-friendly eatery specializing in soba, with a separate sushi bar in the back.

eats.name: Restaurant Kinoshita

eats.note: Although it is Shibuya in terms of address, it is a udon store closer to Shinjuku. It is cost-effective and features homemade udon noodles.

eats.name: Mikore Sushi
eats.note: It is a sushi restaurant located in Shibuya, but close to Shinjuku Station. The lunch special features cost-effectiveness.

eats.name: Cafe Apres-Midi
eats.note: Jazzy cafe with 1960s decor in moody lighting. Excellent food, try the quiche, although portions are small.

eats.name: Beat Cafe
eats.note: Small cafe-bar-restaurant catering to the young alternative rock crowd. While showing constant videos from VH1 Classic on their TV, the easy drinking, simple eating crowd is about as friendly as they

eats.name: Excelsior Cafe
eats.note: Great coffee and delicious sandwiches, with a warm smile.

eats.name: The Aldgate
eats.note: Down to earth smoke-free British-style pub, with a large number of Japanese and international beers on tap and a large collection of British Rock music on vinyl.

eats.name: Hobgoblin Shibuya
eats.note: Outlet of the famous British micro-brewer Wychwood Brewery.

eats.name: Bar Ishinohana
eats.note: Acclaimed high-end bar serving up drinks that are more works of art than cocktails. You may reserve seats from the English webpage.

eats.name: Camelot

eats.name: Club Asia
eats.note: Popular for trance music all night long.

eats.name: Harlem
eats.note: Large two-floor all hip-hop club. Foreigners may not be admitted unless they bring along a Japanese friend.

eats.name: Womb
eats.note: One of Tokyo's largest clubs, designed by the people behind New York's Twilo and the setting of a scene in Babel.

eats.name: Oto
eats.note: Upscale club of mostly locals that have live jazz bands and DJs. Music ranges from jazz, electro, to Euro rock.

eats.name: Rock West
eats.note: A smaller, friendly club that specialised in underground techno, fairly well hidden on 7F of an office building. It's certainly one of the cheaper spots in the area.

eats.note: If you are making an early departure for Kamakura or points south pick up sandwiches to go

eats.name: Kongariya

eats.name: Paul
eats.note: Sandwiches on real baguettes.

eats.name: Yoshinoya
eats.note: Fast food chain with Japanese style food.

eats.name: Atre Shinagawa

eats.name: Devi Corner
eats.note: Excellent Indian cuisine.

eats.name: Royal Host
eats.note: Popular "family restaurant" chain with surprisingly good coffee but little else that stands out.

eats.name: Tsubame Grill (Shinagawa-ekimae)

eats.name: Tikka & Biryani
eats.note: Has excellent Indian Mughal Biryani.

eats.name: 82 Ale House

eats.name: Fight Gyoza
eats.note: Famous for deep-fried gyoza. So many people stand in a line in front of the restaurant.

eats.name: Souten

eats.name: Ghiottone
eats.note: Excellent pasta and salads, in portions that are ample for two. The crab spaghetti is very popular. No non-smoking tables.

eats.name: Malay-Chan
eats.note: A small Malaysian restaurant on the west side of the train/subway station that is a little hard to find. Halal food.

eats.name: Mutekiya
eats.note: Good ramen.

eats.name: Al-Flah
eats.note: A halal supermarket and restaurant that sells halal food, including vegetarian curries. The store also conveniently has a bollywood-movie section.

eats.note: This is a mall dedicated to desserts. Multiple shops and cafes.

eats.name: Nana's Green Tea
eats.note: This cafe has a lot of sweets and drinks made with powdered green tea and adzuki bean. Taste four kinds of Japanese tea. Try the Maccha chocolate latte.

eats.name: Hara-Donut
eats.note: Organic donut shop. Seemingly oxymoronic healthy donuts are made with soy milk.

eats.name: Tonki
eats.note: Possibly good place to go for tonkatsu (breaded deep-fried pork cutlets), and popular with foreigners.

eats.name: Potager
eats.note: A bakery offering vegetable cakes

eats.name: Shutters

eats.name: Jiyugaoka Burger
eats.note: Domestically-sourced, organic and thick burgers in a lush balcony setting.

eats.name: Kochoo
eats.note: Specializes in sundubu, a Korean stew which actually has roots in Los Angeles. All-you-can-eat banchan, which is common practice in Korea but rare in Japan!

eats.name: Mangetsu Korean Cuisine
eats.note: Korean-run establishment with an intimate atmosphere, great for an evening date. Good chijimi!

eats.name: Clann
eats.note: Irish pub with live music many nights.

eats.name: British Restaurant CLASH
eats.note: Formerly known as The Meguro Tavern. A British-style pub with plenty of draft beers and football on the telly.

eats.name: Rakuya
eats.note: Spacious, classy but casual restaurant-bar with live music every night.

eats.name: Speyside Way
eats.note: Hundreds of whiskeys fill every available space. Hundreds. Short selection of micro-beers is also available.

eats.name: Chanko Tomoegata
eats.note: One of Tokyo's oldest chanko joints, operating for over 100 years, specializing in a slightly unusual miso-flavored soup. Lunch sets at ¥840/1260 weekdays/weekends are just about the cheapest chan

eats.name: Asakusa Smile Bar & Cafe

eats.name: Aoi Marushin
eats.note: Tempura, Tempura, Tempura. Aoi Marushin is the largest tempura restaurant in Tokyo!

eats.note: This is a very small, very expensive sushi restaurant in Taito. If you are a sushi buff this is that place for you, with fantastic sushi and great ambiance.

eats.name: Cigars & Cafe LWAN
eats.note: A cigar bar that serves coffee, alcoholic drinks, and desserts. There is a large cigar selection, in particular from the Dominican Republic.

eats.name: Zakuro

eats.name: Fire House
eats.note: A popular hamburger restaurant decorated with American memorabilia.

eats.name: Hantei
eats.note: Serves kushiage (deep fried skewered food) in a rare old wooden building.

eats.name: Tenya
eats.note: Cheap fast-food tempura.

eats.name: Traveler's Dining Pushup

eats.name: Marugo tonkatsu
eats.note: It is a donkatsu shop in Akihabara. It sells high-quality donkatsu even if there is a small amount of money.

eats.name: @home cafe

eats.name: Cure Maid Cafe
eats.note: The original and not quite as over-the-top (or expensive) as some of the competition. A long line can form on weekends.

eats.name: Neko JaLaLa

eats.name: Mitsukoshi and Matsuya Ginza's

eats.name: Nair's
eats.note: The oldest Indian restaurant in Japan, founded in 1949. The Murghee lunch is a favorite: sit back and let the waiter cut up the chicken for you on your plate.

eats.name: Nataraj
eats.note: A terrific Indian vegetarian restaurant in the midst of Ginza, offering an excellent lunch buffet for ¥1050, and beautiful decor as well.

eats.name: Rengatei

eats.name: Chikuyōtei
